video_title: The Death of Reading (with James Marriott) 9/21/26
gist: Russ Roberts talks with James Marriott about his book The New Dark Ages, arguing that the long decline of reading, which began with television, is pushing society toward pre-literate, emotional and less rational public discourse. They cover the history of literacy, the Republic of Letters, why books and screens differ in how they carry ideas, and a pessimistic outlook where reading becomes a deliberate 'cognitive fitness' practice.

insights.claim: Marriott argues that a society moving away from literacy and reading will come to resemble pre-literate societies: more mystical, more emotional, more face-to-face and less mediated by the written word. He draws this from the media theorists Marshall McLuhan and Walter Ong and builds his book 'The New Dark Ages' on it.
insights.speaker: James Marriott
insights.so_what: Frames the decline of reading as a structural regime change in culture and politics, not a passing fad.

insights.claim: Marriott says the book has two themes: the decline of literacy may reverse many Enlightenment gains, which he sees as a product of literacy, and it may push politics back toward pre-literate forms.
insights.speaker: James Marriott
insights.so_what: Long-run political and institutional quality may depend on the dominant information medium.

insights.claim: Marriott says the TV remote and the television era were the start of the shift, not the smartphone. The first statistics showing serious declines in reading date from the 1950s and 1960s, so this is a roughly century-long trend and 'we'll just switch TikTok off' is not a fix.
insights.speaker: James Marriott
insights.so_what: Implies attention-media trends are structural and secular, so policy or app-level fixes are unlikely to reverse them.

insights.claim: Roberts agrees the trend looks inevitable. He expects serious reading to become the habit of a small minority who choose it, and says it is a tough sell to argue for reading on democratic or fun grounds.
insights.speaker: Russ Roberts
insights.so_what: Expect the mass market for long-form text to keep shrinking, with a niche of committed readers.

insights.claim: Literacy was historically rare and fragile. In an ancient Mesopotamian city-state perhaps about 20 people could read and write, it was an elite scribal code, and ancient Rome's literacy rate was probably about 10%. Printing and Protestantism's emphasis on Bible reading then drove mass reading.
insights.speaker: James Marriott
insights.so_what: Mass literacy is a recent historical anomaly, so its erosion is plausible.

insights.claim: Marriott cites a 'reading revolution' in the mid-to-late 18th century, when contemporaries felt that everybody suddenly read novels, almanacs and newspapers. He treats it as the inflection point for the modern literate world and links it to the shift from absolutist monarchies to more democratic politics, though he concedes literacy is not the only factor.
insights.speaker: James Marriott
insights.so_what: Supports his causal link from literacy to democratization, which Roberts doubts.

insights.claim: Roberts is skeptical that mass book access transformed politics as much as claimed, suggesting an inverted-U effect. Books and the internet both democratize information, much of it unreliable, so more information has not obviously meant better political outcomes.
insights.speaker: Russ Roberts
insights.so_what: Counterweight: access to text is not the same as reliable knowledge, which complicates the literacy-causes-better-politics claim.

themes.theme: Why text beats screens for rationality

insights.claim: Marriott argues writing forces more careful ideas and fixes arguments in front of the reader for critical analysis and rereading. Charm, shouting or crying cannot substitute for logic on the page, so books tend to carry more rational and coherent arguments than conversation, video or TikTok.
insights.speaker: James Marriott
insights.so_what: Medium shapes persuasion. Video-first environments reward emotion over logic.

insights.claim: Marriott contrasts Hitler's 'Mein Kampf', found unreadable even by senior Nazis and probably finished by few Germans despite millions of copies sold, with Riefenstahl's film 'Triumph of the Will', regarded as a powerful artistic argument for fascism. His point is that bad ideas launder better through screens than through books because books demand logical form.
insights.speaker: James Marriott
insights.so_what: In a screen-dominated information environment, demagogic ideas face less logical friction.

insights.claim: Marriott says book length and detail push authors toward a more complex picture of their subject, because one-sided polemic becomes tedious beyond about 900 words. Roberts adds that a long biography gives a holistic understanding that cannot be reduced to bullet points, which is the difference between information and knowledge or wisdom.
insights.speaker: James Marriott
insights.so_what: Summaries and short-form content transfer information but not the understanding that comes from long-form reading.

insights.claim: Marriott argues some knowledge, such as history and philosophy as we know them, exists only through books. Kant-style philosophy requires reading, rereading and checking logical connections, and no podcast can convey 600 pages of the history of Prussia. Roberts replies that a good podcast series could teach a lot but could not be made without the books.
insights.speaker: James Marriott
insights.so_what: Audio and video content is parasitic on long-form text for depth.

insights.claim: Marriott, citing Joel Mokyr and Steven Pinker, says the 17th-18th century Republic of Letters, a written network of scientists and thinkers, was a major driver of scientific innovation, growth and the Industrial Revolution. He says Mokyr goes so far as to call it the single cultural fact that explains the Industrial Revolution.
insights.speaker: James Marriott
insights.so_what: Idea-sharing infrastructure with quality norms is a growth input. Degradation of discourse norms could weigh on innovation.

insights.claim: Writing let ideas be judged on merit rather than on the author's dress, accent or class, so the Republic of Letters was democratizing. Marriott also admits it carried a benign elitism, since expressing ideas logically in writing is a minority skill. Roberts adds that its participants' self-imposed norms ('obedience to the unenforceable') kept it producing knowledge rather than rage.
insights.speaker: James Marriott
insights.so_what: Quality norms and entry barriers, not openness alone, make knowledge networks productive, which is a contrast with open social media.

insights.claim: Marriott says reasoning logically, supplying evidence and following arguments to conclusions are products of literacy, not natural human communication. In oral settings persuasion works through entertainment, charm and anger. Walter Ong's observations about oral discourse resemble internet discourse: emotional, face-to-face feeling and logic in the back seat.
insights.speaker: James Marriott
insights.so_what: Explains why evidence-based rebuttals fail online: participants are playing a different game.

insights.claim: Marriott says some post-literate commentators, with Tucker Carlson as his example, act less like print-era public intellectuals explaining the world and more like oral storytellers weaving memorable stories for enraptured audiences. Roberts adds they are not in the truth business, so fact-checking misses the point.
insights.speaker: James Marriott
insights.so_what: Audience attention, not accuracy, is the product. Demanding evidence from such figures does not change behavior.

insights.claim: Marriott says print cooled public discourse. Invective and rhetorical showmanship are fun in person but boring to read at length, so text tends to filter them out. The chilly impersonality of writing is what gave public discourse its rational character, and that is now being lost.
insights.speaker: James Marriott
insights.so_what: Removing the text filter raises the share of heated, emotional content in the public sphere.

themes.theme: Culture, art and the simplification trend

insights.claim: Marriott argues that novels give unique access to other minds. Film shows exteriors and so constantly confronts viewers with difference, while reading shows human similarity, as in abolitionist slave memoirs written for white readers. Roberts partly disagrees, saying great dialogue-driven films and long TV series can approximate this, but agrees film cannot render a character's inner workings.
insights.speaker: James Marriott
insights.so_what: Argues literacy has supported empathy and human-rights movements.

insights.claim: Marriott says great popular songwriters such as Bob Dylan and Paul McCartney were serious readers, and Roberts notes Jagger drew 'Sympathy for the Devil' from Bulgakov's 'The Master and Margarita'. Marriott cites research, which he cannot recall precisely, that pop songs became less lyrically and melodically complex over the last 20 years, and says TikTok virality requires grabbing attention within three or four seconds.
insights.speaker: James Marriott
insights.so_what: Platform mechanics reward immediacy and simplicity, which feeds back into the content produced.

insights.claim: Roberts worries that great works such as Shakespeare, Henry James and Adam Smith will become inaccessible to modern readers, not through illiteracy but through lack of patience and practice. He says his children could barely sit through 'High Noon', so slower older media is also fading.
insights.speaker: Russ Roberts
insights.so_what: Attention-span erosion limits demand for slow, complex content across media.

themes.theme: Cognitive fitness and the future of reading

insights.claim: Marriott predicts that reading's future resembles the post-1960s fitness culture after junk food. As the ambient environment degrades, a minority will deliberately practice 'cognitive fitness', reading difficult books intentionally for set periods, rather than reading as default entertainment.
insights.speaker: James Marriott
insights.so_what: Suggests a premium niche for deliberate-reading products and practices, alongside a shrinking mass market.

insights.claim: Marriott describes himself as a pessimist by profession and temperament and says the long duration of the trend should make us less hopeful. He expects reading to survive but in a more artificial, less inevitable form.
insights.speaker: James Marriott
insights.so_what: Treat declining literacy as a durable secular driver, not a cycle to bet on reversing.
